Here is a comprehensive summary of what is known about the 1906 film The Black Hand.

Basic facts
- Title: The Black Hand (sometimes referenced with slight variations such as The Blackhand)
- Year: 1906
- Country: United States
- Format: Silent, short narrative film (one reel / single-reel length)
- Production company: Biograph Company (Biograph)
- Director: Wallace McCutcheon, Sr. (commonly credited; McCutcheon was Biograph’s principal director in the mid-1900s)
- Genre/themes: Crime/drama; extortion; immigrant communities — an early “Black Hand”/gangster subject
- Status: Surviving prints are known to exist and the film is discussed in histories of early American cinema; it has been preserved and/or circulated in film archives and on compilations of early cinema.

Subject and plot (summary)
- The film depicts a Black Hand extortion plot within an immigrant community. “Black Hand” refers to a style of extortion that was widely reported in U.S. newspapers around the turn of the 20th century, often associated (accurately or not) with Italian or southern European criminal groups who sent threatening, stylized letters demanding money.
- The short dramatizes the terror these letters produced and shows attempts by victims and the community to fight back. As with many one-reel dramas of the period, the narrative is direct and staged in a series of tableaux or scenes: the delivery of the threatening letter, the fear and distress of the family, confrontations with extortionists, and a dramatic resolution (often involving capture or punishment of the criminals).
- The film is notable as one of the earliest American fictional films to take the Black Hand/extortion story as its subject and thus is frequently cited as a proto-gangster film.

Production and style
- Wallace McCutcheon Sr., Biograph’s leading director in the first decade of the 1900s, is credited with the direction; McCutcheon’s work helped shape Biograph’s early narrative style before D. W. Griffith’s arrival.
- The film uses the staged, scenic style of early nickelodeon-era cinema: simulated interior/exterior sets, clearly composed tableaux, and straightforward cross-scene continuity rather than the more modern cinematic grammar that would develop in the 1910s.
- Cinematography in Biograph productions of this period was typically done by cameramen such as G. W. “Billy” Bitzer or others in the Biograph corps, though exact camera credits for many 1906 shorts are not always recorded.

Historical significance
- The Black Hand is often mentioned in film histories as one of the earliest cinematic treatments of urban organized-crime/extortion themes and is therefore sometimes referred to in discussions of the origins of the gangster film.
- The subject matter shows how early American cinema responded to contemporary news stories and public anxieties about immigration, crime, and urban life; the film is an example of early cinema’s engagement with “topical” melodrama.
- It is also part of the larger Biograph output that helped invent and popularize narrative filmmaking practices in the United States.

Preservation and availability
- Prints survive in film archives and the title appears in archive catalogs and filmographic references. Because it is an early Biograph short, it has circulated in film-historical compilations and may be available through archive websites, DVD collections of early films, or video platforms that host public-domain early cinema.
- Specific holdings: archival catalogs (for example, the Library of Congress and other film archives that collect Biograph material) list early Biograph films; consult those catalogs or published filmographies for exact holdings and viewing access.

Sources and further reading
- General histories of early American cinema and Biograph for context: Charles Musser’s work on early American film and studio practice; Tom Gunning’s writings on early cinema spectatorship and the “cinema of attractions”; Richard Abel’s histories of early film.
- Filmographies and catalogs: Kemp R. Niver’s or the Library of Congress’s catalogs of early motion pictures; the AFI Catalog and other reference works on American film may list the title.
- Scholarly articles about early representations of crime and the “Black Hand” in popular culture discuss films like this as part of a broader media response to ethnicized crime narratives in the early 20th century.

Caveats and uncertainties
- Records from 1906 are sometimes incomplete. Precise cast lists, running time in minutes (beyond “one reel”/short), and some production credits are not always documented definitively in surviving records.
- Because multiple short films of the era dealt with extortion or “Black Hand” themes, be careful when consulting secondary references to ensure they refer specifically to the 1906 Biograph short directed by Wallace McCutcheon Sr. and not to other similarly titled productions from later years.
